AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.title: The exact potential and average smoothness constants
AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.summary:
The state space is \(\mathbb R^p\). Every derivative and smoothness constant is computed from one real-valued potential. Coordinate smoothness uses the literal supremum of the Taylor quotients in the coordinate definition; it is not a supplied error bound. The deterministic results assume differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient, without adding a Hessian or third derivative assumption.

\[M_j=\sup_{x,\ a\ne0}\frac{2(f(x+ae_j)-f(x)-a\,\partial_j f(x))}{a^2},\qquad M_{\rm av}=\frac1p\sum_jM_j.\]

Formal correspondence. The state type is EuclideanSpace over Fin p; the coordinate definition corresponds to source label coordM.

steps.title: Euclidean coordinates and literal Taylor quotients
steps.body: The state space is \(\mathbb R^p\), and \(e_j\) is its \(j\)th unit vector. The coordinate Taylor quotient is twice the difference between \(f(x+ae_j)\) and its first order approximation at \(x\), divided by \(a^2\). The defining set ranges over every \(x\) and every nonzero real \(a\). Its supremum is exactly \(M_j\), and the average of these \(p\) constants is \(M_{\rm av}\). A displacement \(a=1\) at \(x=0\) proves that every coordinate quotient set is nonempty. The unit norm and coordinate inner-product identities connect these definitions to Euclidean calculus.

steps.title: The actual global gradient seminorm
steps.body: The global gradient seminorm is the supremum of the gradient difference norm divided by the state difference norm over unequal states. For \(p\) positive, a pair consisting of zero and one coordinate vector witnesses nonemptiness. Any supplied gradient Lipschitz constant \(M\) bounds every quotient, so it bounds the supremum. The quotients are nonnegative, hence the supremum is nonnegative. Conversely, each quotient is at most this bounded supremum. Multiplying by the strictly positive state difference norm proves that the gradient is Lipschitz with its exact seminorm. Thus subsequent inequalities may use the literal constant in the paper instead of an arbitrary larger bound.

steps.title: Bound and attain the coordinate quadratic model
steps.body: The shared differentiable descent lemma gives an upper quadratic model with coefficient \(M/2\). At a coordinate displacement \(ae_j\), the inner product is \(a\) times the \(j\)th gradient coordinate and the squared displacement norm is \(a^2\). For nonzero \(a\), multiply the upper model by \(2\) and divide by \(a^2\) to show that every Taylor quotient is at most \(M\). This proves boundedness of the quotient set and \(M_j\) at most \(M\). Each quotient is also at most its supremum \(M_j\). Multiplication by \(a^2\) and rearrangement recover the sharper coordinate upper model with coefficient \(M_j/2\). The zero displacement follows directly. No existence of a second derivative is needed.

steps.title: Compare strong convexity, average smoothness and global smoothness
steps.body: The strong-convexity lower model at zero and \(e_j\) gives the same first order term as the coordinate upper model, with quadratic coefficients \(m/2\) and \(M_j/2\) respectively. Subtraction yields \(m\) at most \(M_j\). Summing the upper and lower bounds over the \(p\) coordinates and dividing by positive \(p\) proves \(m\) at most \(M_{\rm av}\) at most \(M\). Apply the upper bounds to the actual nonnegative global gradient seminorm, using its proved Lipschitz property, to obtain \(M_j\) at most \(M_\infty\) and \(M_{\rm av}\) at most \(M_\infty\) with exactly the paper's supremum constants.

steps.title: Actual Hessian, Laplacian and finite-sum notation
steps.body:
The Hessian is the second Fréchet derivative evaluated on pairs of coordinate vectors, and the Laplacian is its canonical trace. Expanding the Laplacian in the canonical orthonormal basis gives exactly the matrix trace of this Hessian. The Laplacian smoothness assumption requires three continuous derivatives and the displayed bound on the squared norm of the gradient of the Laplacian, with the factor \(p\) from (lip:2). It does not introduce a Hessian Lipschitz requirement. Finally, the root mean square component smoothness is the square root of the average of the squared exact component-gradient seminorms, as in (eq:Mtwo).

Formal correspondence. The exact definitions are hessian, laplacian, LaplacianSmooth and rmsComponentSmoothness; the Laplacian is the Mathlib operator.

AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.title: The deterministic gradient-step and descent lemmas
AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.summary:
The two estimates here concern the actual gradient of the potential. The first uses only strong convexity and differentiability, and the second uses only differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient. Both are proved on arbitrary real Hilbert spaces and therefore apply to the paper's Euclidean space. The proofs also cover the zero step size.

\[\|x-h\nabla f(x)-y\|^2\le(1-mh)\|x-y\|^2+2h(f(y)-f(x))+h^2\|\nabla f(x)\|^2.\]

steps.title: The gradient-step lemma (eq:basic-gd)
steps.body: Expand the squared distance after the deterministic gradient step: the result is the original squared distance minus twice \(h\) times the inner product of the displacement and the gradient, plus \(h^2\) times the squared gradient norm. The supporting-plane inequality for \(m\)-strong convexity bounds the negative inner product by \(f(y)-f(\theta)\) minus \(m/2\) times the squared displacement norm. Multiply that inequality by the nonnegative scalar \(2h\) and substitute it in the expansion. Collecting the squared-distance coefficients gives \(1-mh\), precisely the paper's displayed gradient-step lemma.

steps.title: Deterministic descent in the smoothing lemma (eq:exp-upper)
steps.body: Apply the shared quadratic upper model for a differentiable potential with \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient at the point \(\theta-h\nabla f(\theta)\). Its first order term is minus \(h\) times the squared gradient norm, and the quadratic remainder is \(Mh^2/2\) times that norm. Multiply by two and factor to obtain minus \(h\) times \((2-hM)\) times the squared gradient norm. If \(hM\le2\), this right side is nonpositive, which proves that the gradient step does not increase the potential. This verifies the deterministic conclusion of the paper's smoothing lemma; it does not assert the separate expectation inequality for random noise.

AverageLMC/Recurrence.lean.title: Exact scalar contraction and recurrence iteration
AverageLMC/Recurrence.lean.summary: Write \(r_k=(m/p)W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\), \(t=mh\), and \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1\) when the dimension is positive. This module proves implications for arbitrary real sequences satisfying the displayed scalar recurrence. It does not construct an LMC law, establish its Wasserstein one-step inequality, or infer that inequality from convexity and smoothness. Its constant-step conclusion is the scalar arithmetic underlying Theorem 1; its harmonic induction is the decreasing-step calculation in Proposition 1.

steps.title: Bound the rational contraction by the exponential
steps.body: For \(0\le t\le1\), prove \[(1-t)/(1+t)\le e^{-2t}.\] At the endpoint \(t=1\), the left side is zero and the exponential is positive. For \(t<1\), both \(1-t\) and \(1+t\) are positive. The first term of the established logarithmic series lower bound gives \[t\le\tfrac12\log\frac{1+t}{1-t}.\] Since the two rational fractions are reciprocals, their logarithms have opposite signs. Thus \(\log((1-t)/(1+t))\le-2t\); monotonicity of the exponential proves the desired estimate. The proof handles \(t=0\) directly within the non-strict branch, so no positive-step assumption is added.

steps.title: Iterate an affine inequality up to a finite horizon
steps.body: Let \(q\ge0\) and \(c\ge0\). If \(r_{j+1}\le q r_j+(1-q)c\) is known only for \(j<n\), induction proves the stronger finite-horizon identity-shaped bound \[r_k\le q^k r_0+(1-q^k)c\qquad(0\le k\le n).\] The successor proof multiplies the preceding bound by nonnegative \(q\), inserts the one-step assumption, and expands \(q^{k+1}=q^kq\). Since \(q^nc\ge0\), discarding the correction \(-q^nc\) yields \(r_n\le q^nr_0+c\). No contraction condition \(q<1\) is needed for this algebraic statement. The finite-horizon hypothesis is essential for the warmup application, where the schedule changes after a prescribed time.

steps.title: Resolve the constant-step recurrence with the paper's bias constant
steps.body: Assume \(a\ge0\), \(0\le t\le1\), \(r_0\ge0\), and \[r_{j+1}\le\frac{1-t}{1+t}r_j+\frac{at^2}{1+t}.\] Put \(q=(1-t)/(1+t)\) and \(c=at/2\). Positive \(1+t\) makes \(q\ge0\), and rational algebra gives exactly \[\frac{at^2}{1+t}=(1-q)\frac{at}{2}.\] Apply the finite-horizon affine lemma. Raising the previously proved inequality \(q\le e^{-2t}\) to the natural power \(n\), and using \((e^{-2t})^n=e^{-2tn}\), bounds the initial-error contribution. Its multiplication by \(r_0\) uses the explicit nonnegativity hypothesis. Therefore \[r_n\le e^{-2tn}r_0+\frac{at}{2}.\] The finite-horizon result assumes the recurrence only before \(n\); its global specialization assumes it at every natural time. In unnormalized paper notation the bias equals \((M_{\mathrm{av}}+m)hp/(2m)\). This interpretation is an algebraic substitution, not a proved stochastic endpoint in these files.

steps.title: Close the decreasing-step induction exactly
steps.body: For \(x\ge1\), the coefficient \(q_x=(1-1/x)/(1+1/x)\) is nonnegative. Hence \(r\le a/x\) implies \[q_xr+\frac{a/x^2}{1+1/x}\le q_x\frac ax+\frac{a/x^2}{1+1/x}=\frac a{x+1}.\] The equality follows by clearing the positive denominators and expanding products. The local lemma does not require \(a\ge0\). For the tail theorem, let \(\kappa\ge1\), initialize \(r_0\le a/\kappa\), and assume the given recurrence uses \(t_n=1/(\kappa+n)\). Natural induction applies the local lemma at \(x=\kappa+n\), proving \[r_n\le\frac a{\kappa+n}.\] The tail theorem retains \(a\ge0\), consistent with \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1\). This conclusion is conditional on the scalar recurrence; it does not supply its analytic source.

AverageLMC/Complexity.lean.title: Proposition 1: scalar warmup, variable steps and iteration count
AverageLMC/Complexity.lean.summary: Use \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1>0\), \(\kappa=\kappa_{\max}\ge1\), and \(\varepsilon_0>0\). The paper's exact positive logarithm, warmup ceiling, decreasing-step schedule and accuracy ceiling are represented explicitly. Given \(0\le r_0\le\varepsilon_0^2\) and the normalized scalar one-step recurrence, the module proves \(r_k\le a/(\kappa+k-k_0)\) for \(k\ge k_0\), then \(r_k\le\varepsilon^2\) at the stated iteration count. All stochastic, coupling and Wasserstein facts needed to establish that recurrence remain external proof obligations.

steps.title: Encode the exact positive logarithm and two-phase schedule
steps.body:
The definitions are \[\log_+(z)=\max\{\log z,0\},\qquad k_0=\left\lceil\frac\kappa2\log_+\!\left(\frac{2\kappa\varepsilon_0^2}{a}\right)\right\rceil,\qquad t_k=\frac1{\kappa+(k-k_0)_+}.\] The ceiling is the least nonnegative integer above the displayed value, and \((k-k_0)_+\) is the nonnegative part of the integer difference. Thus the difference is exactly zero before warmup ends; for \(k\ge k_0\) it is the ordinary integer difference. The dimensionless step \(t_k=mh_k\) corresponds to the paper's \(h_k=1/(M_{\max}+m(k-k_0)_+)\). These are definitions, with no hidden decay or convergence assumptions.

Formal correspondence. Lean represents the ceiling with the natural-number ceiling and the positive part by natural subtraction followed by a real cast.

steps.title: Verify the smoothness restriction for the full schedule
steps.body: For \(\kappa>0\), the cast natural difference is nonnegative, so \(\kappa+(k-k_0)_+\ge\kappa>0\). Positivity of the reciprocal and monotonicity of reciprocals give \[0<t_k\le1/\kappa.\] When \(\kappa=\kappa_{\max}=M_{\max}/m\), this is the arithmetic behind \(h_kM_{\max}\le1\). It verifies the schedule's restriction for every step, including those in the warmup phase; it does not assert the one-step stochastic inequality itself.

steps.title: Use the warmup ceiling to reduce the initial error
steps.body: Let \(R=2\kappa\varepsilon_0^2/a>0\). The natural ceiling gives \[k_0\ge\frac\kappa2\max\{\log R,0\}\ge\frac\kappa2\log R.\] Multiplying and dividing by the positive \(\kappa\) yields \(-2k_0/\kappa\le-\log R\). Exponentiate this inequality and multiply by the nonnegative \(\varepsilon_0^2\): \[e^{-2k_0/\kappa}\varepsilon_0^2\le e^{-\log R}\varepsilon_0^2=\frac a{2\kappa}.\] The final equality uses \(e^{\log R}=R\) on its verified positive domain and cancels nonzero parameters. The same proof covers \(R\le1\), where the positive logarithm is zero and the warmup length can vanish.

steps.title: Join warmup to the harmonic tail
steps.body: Assume \(0\le r_0\le\varepsilon_0^2\) and, for every natural \(k\), \[r_{k+1}\le\frac{1-t_k}{1+t_k}r_k+\frac{at_k^2}{1+t_k},\qquad t_k=\frac1{\kappa+(k-k_0)_+}.\] Before \(k_0\), natural subtraction gives \(t_k=1/\kappa\). The finite-horizon constant-step theorem therefore gives \[r_{k_0}\le e^{-2k_0/\kappa}r_0+\frac a{2\kappa}\le\frac a\kappa,\] where the second inequality uses the initialization bound and the warmup-decay lemma. Shift the sequence to \(s_n=r_{k_0+n}\). Cancellation of the natural subtraction gives \(t_{k_0+n}=1/(\kappa+n)\), so the harmonic tail theorem applies and proves \(s_n\le a/(\kappa+n)\). For any \(k\ge k_0\), choose \(n=k-k_0\) and use \(k_0+(k-k_0)=k\), obtaining \[r_k\le\frac a{\kappa+(k-k_0)}.\] This is precisely the scalar calculation in the proof of Proposition 1, with the recurrence kept as an explicit hypothesis rather than disguised as a convexity or smoothness assumption.

steps.title: Verify the accuracy ceiling and conclude the conditional rate
steps.body: The exact iteration threshold is \[k_\varepsilon=k_0+\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac a{\varepsilon^2}-\kappa,0\right\}\right\rceil.\] Suppose \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(k\ge k_\varepsilon\). Natural arithmetic first gives \(k\ge k_0\) and then bounds \(k-k_0\) below by that ceiling. After casting to \(\mathbb R\), \[k-k_0\ge\max\{a/\varepsilon^2-\kappa,0\}\ge a/\varepsilon^2-\kappa.\] Thus \(\kappa+(k-k_0)\ge a/\varepsilon^2\). Both denominators used in rearrangement are positive, proving \[\frac a{\kappa+(k-k_0)}\le\varepsilon^2.\] The arithmetic envelope theorem proves this implication without a recurrence. The final accuracy theorem combines it with the preceding conditional scalar Proposition 1 to obtain \(r_k\le\varepsilon^2\). It proves no independent assertion that actual LMC errors obey the required recurrence.

AverageLMC.lean.title: Main average-smoothness sampling theorems
AverageLMC.lean.summary: This import bundle exports the Gaussian LMC, decreasing-step LMC, Laplacian LMC and control-variate SGLD bounds. Their coordinate-average smoothness constants, analytic estimates and distributional recurrences are proved. The source inventory distinguishes the main sampling results from broader auxiliary coverage.

AverageLMC/Check.lean.title: Audit the main sampling proofs and analytic dependencies
AverageLMC/Check.lean.summary:
The audit brings together the sampling convergence theorems and the analytic estimates used in their proofs.

Formal audit. The audit imports the main sampling development and prints the axioms used by its distributional endpoints and analytic bridges. Only standard Lean mathematical foundations are expected. The separate coverage verifier checks the exact source inventory and the main-theorem review scope.

AverageLMC/SquaredTransport.lean.title: Coupling lifts and the squared transport infimum
AverageLMC/SquaredTransport.lean.summary:
The SGLD argument begins with any finite-cost coupling of the full-gradient output and the Gibbs target. A regular conditional distribution lifts this coupling to the original initialization and Gaussian space. No optimal coupling is assumed.

\[W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty,\quad r\le a\,C(\gamma)^2+b\quad\hbox{for every finite-cost coupling }\gamma\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r\le aW_2(\mu,\pi)^2+b.\]

steps.title: Pass real quadratic estimates through the infimum
steps.body: For a nonnegative coefficient, choose finite couplings with costs arbitrarily close to the Wasserstein infimum and pass to the limit by continuity. For a negative coefficient, any finite coupling suffices: multiplication reverses the comparison between its squared cost and the infimum. The transport specialization retains an explicit finiteness condition for the output before its real value is used.

steps.title: Disintegrate the output coupling over its first marginal
steps.body: The conditional kernel of the chosen coupling is composed with the original output map. Integrating this kernel against the original input law constructs a probability measure on input and target. Its input marginal is the original law. Mapping input and target to output and target recovers the chosen coupling, by the disintegration identity; taking its second marginal therefore recovers the Gibbs target. These identities justify adding an independent stochastic-gradient index to an actual output coupling.

AverageLMC/CenteredPerturbation.lean.title: Centered perturbations add their actual variance to transport
AverageLMC/CenteredPerturbation.lean.summary:
A square-integrable perturbation with zero conditional mean may be added to a measurable full-gradient output. This module constructs every required coupling and proves the variance addition estimate used by SGLD.

\[\mathbb E[D\mid S]=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad W_2^2(\mathcal L(F(S)+D),\pi)\le W_2^2(\mathcal L(F(S)),\pi)+\mathbb E\|D\|^2.\]

steps.title: Translate quadratic transport cost into an ordinary integral
steps.body: The square of the real \(L^{2}\) seminorm is the integral of the squared norm. Square integrability supplies finiteness, so taking the real value cannot discard an infinite cost.

steps.title: Lift, expand and cancel the cross term
steps.body: Disintegrate each finite-cost output coupling to the original input, and extend it by the independent index law. Expand the squared displacement after adding the perturbation. Fubini and the continuous linear functional given by inner product with the fixed displacement turn the cross term into the inner product with the conditional mean, which is zero. The remaining two energies are the original coupling cost and the actual perturbation second moment. Passing this bound through all finite coupling costs proves the squared Wasserstein inequality.

AverageLMC/ExtendedTransport.lean.title: Main bounds for arbitrary probability initializations
AverageLMC/ExtendedTransport.lean.summary:
Main sampling statements use extended nonnegative transport, allowing an infinite initial second moment. Their finite-distance real versions are convenient for the analytic proofs.

\[W_2^2(\mu',\pi')\le aW_2^2(\mu,\pi)+b,\qquad a>0,\ b\ge0,\]

The inequality is interpreted in the extended nonnegative reals, including infinite initial distance.

steps.title: Extend a positive affine squared bound to infinity
steps.body: Split on finiteness of the initial Wasserstein distance. In the finite case, derive output finiteness and embed the nonnegative real estimate into the extended nonnegative reals, preserving squared costs and nonnegative arithmetic. If the initial distance is infinite, the strictly positive contraction coefficient makes the right side infinite. Thus the main endpoint needs no independent moment assumption.

AverageLMC/SGLDLaw.lean.title: The actual independent Gaussian and finite-index SGLD law
AverageLMC/SGLDLaw.lean.summary:
The transition is the manuscript's fixed-point control-variate update. Its input measure is the independent product of initialization, a standard Gaussian innovation, and the uniform component index.

\[X^+=X-hn\big(\nabla f_I(X)-\nabla f_I(\theta_*)\big)+\sqrt{2h}\,Z,\qquad I\sim{\rm Unif}\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad Z\sim N(0,I_p).\]

steps.title: Define the update and propagate probability laws
steps.body: The proposal subtracts \(h\) times \(n\) times the difference between the selected component gradients at the current state and the anchor, then adds the Gaussian innovation. Mapping the product measure defines one transition; iteration defines all marginal laws. Algebra separates the full-gradient proposal and the centered estimator error. Lipschitz gradients give measurability, and the positive finite index count gives normalization of all these laws.

steps.title: Derive the required second moments
steps.body: A Lipschitz score acts on every \(L^{2}\) input, including its nonzero value at the origin. The Gaussian proposal is a sum of the input, its scaled score and independent Gaussian noise, so it lies in \(L^{2}\). Adding the finite-index estimator error proves a second moment for the actual SGLD output law.

steps.title: Apply the constructed centered-perturbation coupling
steps.body: Instantiate the general variance-addition theorem on initialization times Gaussian innovation. The perturbation is minus \(h\) times the estimator error, whose index mean is zero by the proved unbiasedness identity. Pulling \(h^2\) through its norm integral gives the actual SGLD transport bound. Fubini removes the unused Gaussian variable and identifies the remaining variance as estimator energy minus full-gradient energy.

steps.title: Recover the manuscript's component-energy term
steps.body: The exact uniform-index identity makes estimator energy equal to \(n\) times the sum of squared component-gradient increments. Each increment is square integrable by its Lipschitz score bound, justifying interchange of the finite sum and the initial-law integral.

AverageLMC/SGLDRecurrence.lean.title: The scalar SGLD contraction with the printed constants
AverageLMC/SGLDRecurrence.lean.summary:
Here \(m\) is the full curvature, \(R=n\) times the component RMS seminorm, and \(A\) is the full coordinate average. These scalar lemmas are applied to the actual-law recurrence in SGLDTheorem.

\[3R^2h\le m,\quad m^2\le R^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1-mh}{1+mh}+2R^2h^2\le\frac1{1+mh}.\]

steps.title: Compare the exact contraction and bias coefficients
steps.body: The restriction \(3R^2h\le m\), together with \(m^2\le R^2\), implies \(mh\le1/3\). Multiplying by the positive denominator \(1+mh\) bounds the actual contraction by its reciprocal. The same step restriction bounds the persistent-error coefficient by the precise expression \(A+2m+2R^2/m\), divided by \(1+mh\).

steps.title: Iterate around the exact fixed floor
steps.body: Set \(q=(1+mh)^{-1}\) and \(c=(A+2m+2R^2/m)hp/m\). The previous comparisons put the actual recursion below \(q\) times its preceding value plus \((1-q)c\). The finite-horizon affine induction gives \(q^k\) times the initial value plus \(c\), including the zero-step case.

AverageLMC/SGLDTheorem.lean.title: SGLD convergence for the actual control-variate chain
AverageLMC/SGLDTheorem.lean.summary:
The stochastic inputs are the component potentials and the independent Gaussian/index transition, with the anchor equal to the true minimizer. No transport recurrence or invariant law is supplied as a premise.

\[0\le h\le\frac{\bar m}{3nM_{\rm rms}^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\le(1+n\bar m h)^{-k}W_2^2(\nu_0,\pi)+\left(M_{\rm av}(f/n)+2\bar m+\frac{2M_{\rm rms}^2}{\bar m}\right)\frac{hp}{\bar m}.\]

steps.title: Derive the unrestricted one-step claim
steps.body: Combine the actual average-smoothness LMC inequality with variance addition. The exact variance identity subtracts one full-gradient energy from estimator energy. The leftover coefficient is at most \(h^2(hM-2)/(1+mh)\), because the discarded term is nonpositive. This gives Proposition 3's first estimate for every nonnegative step, with its actual estimator-energy term.

steps.title: Obtain the RMS recurrence and propagate finite transport
steps.body: When \(hM\le2\), drop the nonpositive score term. The exact component RMS bounds estimator energy by \(R^2\) times the initial squared radius about the minimizer. The radius estimate is twice the squared transport error plus \(2p/m\), yielding exactly the second claim's coefficients. Actual proposals preserve \(L^{2}\) and probability, so finite quadratic transport propagates along every iteration.

steps.title: Prove the constant-step main theorem
steps.body: The full gradient has Lipschitz constant at most the exact \(R=n\) \(M_{\rm rms}\), and strong convexity gives \(m\) at most \(R\). The paper's step restriction therefore ensures the local stability condition. Apply the proved scalar recurrence to the actual SGLD marginal laws. The result has the reciprocal contraction and the precise persistent error \(A+2m+2R^2/m\). Substituting \(m=n\bar m\) and dividing the full average by \(n\) produces the printed theorem in average-potential units.

steps.title: Remove a finite-moment hypothesis from the main statement
steps.body: The extended endpoint applies the positive-affine transport extension. It has the same contraction, step restriction and average-potential constants for every probability initialization. For infinite initial distance its right side is infinite; otherwise all moments used by the real proof are derived from finite transport to the Gibbs target. The source-facing paper endpoint uses the literal coordinate average of the divided potential \(f/n\). Gradient linearity rescales every coordinate Taylor quotient, and the proved homogeneity of their exact suprema identifies this constant with the full average divided by \(n\), without a chosen replacement bound.

AverageLMC/LaplacianWeakChain.lean.title: Weighted weak consistency for the actual iid Euler chain
AverageLMC/LaplacianWeakChain.lean.summary:
The local compact-\(C^{2}\) expansion is lifted to genuine stochastic Euler transitions while retaining arbitrary bounded measurable information about the initialization. All independence statements refer to actual Gaussian joint laws.

\[|a_{k+1}-a_k-hc_k|\le E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left|a_n-a_0-\sum_{kHere the preceding lemmas derive the local residual for actual independent Gaussian Euler steps.

steps.title: Integrate a fresh Gaussian step with its retained past weight
steps.body: Bounded observations times a bounded weight are integrable. The joint product law of weight, state and next innovation lets the update expectation be rewritten as its actual conditional Gaussian integral, by mapping measures and applying Fubini. Applying the uniform pointwise \(C^{2}\) expansion gives a weighted one-step residual with the same \(K\) at every state and mesh.

steps.title: Retain the weight through the real Euler recursion
steps.body: Adjoin the initial weight as a passive coordinate of the noise-driven chain. The ordinary iid recursion theorem supplies its product joint law with the next innovation. Passive-coordinate retention and the almost-everywhere representation of the \(L^{2}\) Euler chain transfer that law to the actual quotient-valued process. The generator formula and the exact \(L^{2}\) drift norm then give the genuine one-step weak residual.

steps.title: Sum a uniform local error over the full time horizon
steps.body: The signed local residuals telescope to final expectation minus initial expectation minus the generator Riemann sum. The triangle inequality bounds the sum by the number of steps times a common local bound. A single \(L^{2}\) drift radius controls every mesh state, so the resulting error is \(AT(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)(1+R^2)\). This supplies the discrete stochastic input for the deterministic Euler-to-Dynkin limit.

AverageLMC/Smoothing.lean.title: Smoothing by arbitrary independent centered coordinates
AverageLMC/Smoothing.lean.summary: This module proves the full expectation conclusion of the manuscript smoothing lemma. The coordinates may have any distributions with zero mean and unit second moment; Gaussianity is used only in the final specialization. The bound uses the exact coordinate Taylor suprema and their arithmetic average. All potential, score, and product integrability follows from the supplied coordinate second moments and the gradient Lipschitz assumption.

steps.title: Build square-integrable partial coordinate sums
steps.body: For a finite set \(S\) of coordinate indices, define \(Z_S\) as the sum of \(\xi_j\) \(e_j\) over \(j\) in \(S\). Each scalar coordinate is square integrable, and the map \(a\) to \(ae_j\) is continuous linear, so every vector summand and every finite partial sum is square integrable. The actual gradient evaluated at an \(L^{2}\) state is also \(L^{2}\): apply the existing Lipschitz drift lift to the canonical \(L^{2}\) representative, then transfer back along its almost-everywhere equality. Adding the deterministic center and scaling preserve these moments.

steps.title: Insert one independent coordinate and eliminate its linear term
steps.body:
Induct on the finite coordinate set. When inserting \(i\) outside \(S\), apply the exact coordinate model at \(x+c\) \(Z_S\) with displacement \(c\) \(\xi_i\). It gives

\[f(x+cZ_{S\cup\{i\}})\le f(x+cZ_S)+c\xi_i\partial_i f(x+cZ_S)+\tfrac12 M_i c^2\xi_i^2.\]

Independence of the scalar coordinates survives the maps \(a\) to \(ae_j\). Consequently their partial vector sum is independent of the new coordinate. Composing with the actual gradient coordinate proves independence of \(\xi_i\) and the displayed derivative term. Their product is integrable by the \(L^{2}\) Holder inequality, and its integral factors; the zero first moment makes it vanish. The quadratic term integrates to \(M_i\) \(c^2/2\). Adding this to the inductive bound proves the finite-set estimate, with no assumed stochastic error inequality.

steps.title: Sum every coordinate and recover the exact average-smoothness coefficient
steps.body:
For the full index set, the coordinate sum is exactly the Euclidean vector with coordinates \(\xi_j\). Choose \(c\) equal to the square root of \(2s\), whose square is \(2s\) because \(s\) is nonnegative. Smooth potentials have quadratic growth, so the perturbed potential and its difference from the deterministic center are integrable. The finite-set theorem yields

\[\mathbb E[f(x+\sqrt{2s}\,\xi)-f(x)]\le s\sum_j M_j=M_{\rm av}ps.\]

The final equality uses the literal definition \(M_{\mathrm{av}}=p^{-1}\sum_jM_j\) and the positive dimension.

steps.title: Specialize to the actual standard Gaussian measure
steps.body: Take the product of \(n=p\) real Gaussian laws with mean zero and variance one. Each coordinate evaluation preserves its marginal Gaussian measure; the product coordinates are mutually independent, square integrable, centered, and have second moment one. Apply the arbitrary-coordinate theorem on this product. Its pushforward is identified by the Euclidean coordinate map with the actual standard Gaussian law, so the change-of-measure integral is precisely the Gaussian smoothing integral used by the LMC transition.

AverageLMC/ExpectedGradientStep.lean.title: Expected potential and gradient-step energies on \(L^{2}\)
AverageLMC/ExpectedGradientStep.lean.summary: The deterministic gradient-step and descent inequalities extend to the actual Hilbert space of square-integrable random variables. Potential integrability is proved from quadratic growth, and the lifted drift is identified almost everywhere with the pointwise gradient. These estimates retain the full gradient energy, including its sign-sensitive correction in the sampler one-step bound.

steps.title: Integrate the strong gradient-step inequality
steps.body:
Apply the integrated strong supporting-plane inequality to \(Y\) and \(X\). Reverse the displacement \(Y\)-\(X\) to \(X\)-\(Y\) and multiply by nonnegative \(h\). Expand the squared \(L^{2}\) distance after subtracting \(h\) times the lifted gradient. The mixed inner product is bounded by the potential difference and strong convexity, giving

\[\|X-h\nabla f(X)-Y\|_{L^2}^2\le(1-mh)\|X-Y\|_{L^2}^2+2h(\mathbb Ef(Y)-\mathbb Ef(X))+h^2\|\nabla f(X)\|_{L^2}^2.\]

The norms are genuine \(L^{2}\) norms and every expectation is finite.

steps.title: Integrate deterministic descent without dropping the score term
steps.body:
The pointwise deterministic descent theorem holds outside a null set where the lifted state arithmetic and lifted gradient agree with their ordinary representatives. Both potential terms are integrable by smooth quadratic growth, and the squared score is integrable by the Lipschitz drift construction. Integrate the pointwise estimate, use linearity, and identify the integral of the squared lifted gradient with its squared \(L^{2}\) norm. The result is

\[2(\mathbb Ef(X-h\nabla f(X))-\mathbb Ef(X))\le-h(2-hM)\|\nabla f(X)\|_{L^2}^2.\]

AverageLMC/ScoreMoment.lean.title: Exact average-smoothness Gibbs score and Laplacian moments
AverageLMC/ScoreMoment.lean.summary: The first-order part proves \(\mathbb E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2\le pM_{\rm av}\) without assuming any Hessian or integration-by-parts identity. The second part proves Lemma 7 for \(C^{2}\) convex potentials with finite Gibbs normalization: the true score energy equals the \(L^{1}\) Laplacian integral, bounded by the exact Laplacian supremum and then the exact average coordinate smoothness. Strong convexity supplies normalization automatically in the main application.

steps.title: Obtain the exact coordinate score MGF by translation
steps.body:
The coordinate quadratic model implies

\[e^{-f(x)}e^{-a\partial_j f(x)}\le e^{M_j a^2/2}e^{-f(x+ae_j)}.\]

Integrate the nonnegative functions against Lebesgue measure. Translation invariance leaves the partition function unchanged, and finite positive normalization cancels it. Replacing a by minus \(t\) produces the Gaussian MGF bound for the actual \(j\)th score coordinate, with proxy \(M_j\). The same finite exponential integral bound supplies exponential integrability, so this is an actual sub-Gaussian statement rather than a formal integral comparison.

steps.title: Sum sharp second moments without second differentiability
steps.body:
Strong convexity implies \(m\) at most every coordinate Taylor supremum, so each \(M_j\) is nonnegative. Apply the established sub-Gaussian second-moment theorem to the coordinate score: its uncentered second moment is at most \(M_j\), and square integrability is derived at the same time. The squared Euclidean norm is the sum of the squared coordinates. Integral linearity and the finite sum therefore give

\[\mathbb E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2\le\sum_j M_j=pM_{\rm av}.\]

Only differentiability, a Lipschitz gradient, and positive strong convexity are used in this sharper score bound.

steps.title: Identify coordinate derivatives and control all weighted integrals
steps.body: A normalized Gibbs integral is integrable exactly when its exponential-weighted Lebesgue integrand is integrable, since the partition function is finite and positive. The coordinate score equals the directional Frechet derivative in \(e_j\). Differentiating that expression identifies its derivative in \(e_j\) with the actual diagonal Hessian entry. \(C^{2}\) regularity makes this coordinate score \(C^{1}\). Projecting the global gradient Lipschitz inequality bounds the coordinate score with the same Lipschitz constant, and hence bounds its derivative. These facts justify the weighted integration by parts used next.

steps.title: Prove the score-Hessian identity by global integration by parts
steps.body:
Set \(\psi\) equal to the \(j\)th score coordinate. Its first and second moments are finite by the first-order Gibbs score theorem. Its directional derivative is bounded by \(M\), so that derivative is Gibbs integrable as well. The three unnormalized functions needed for global integration by parts are therefore integrable: the derivative of \(\psi\) times \(e^{-f}\), \(\psi\) times the derivative of \(e^{-f}\), and \(\psi e^{-f}\). The chain rule gives \(D_je^{-f}=-e^{-f}\psi\). Integration by parts cancels its minus sign and proves

\[\int(\partial_j f)^2\,d\pi=\int\partial_{jj}f\,d\pi.\]

No decay or boundary term is supplied as a hypothesis. Summing the finite coordinate identities and using \(\operatorname{tr}(D^2f)=\Delta f\) proves the full score-Laplacian identity. The partition-based statement works whenever normalization is finite; strong convexity supplies normalization automatically.

steps.title: Differentiate the coordinate quadratic model to bound each Hessian diagonal
steps.body: Apply the coordinate upper model at \(x\) with displacement \(ae_j\) and at \(x+ae_j\) with displacement minus \(ae_j\). Addition gives \(a\) times the difference of the coordinate scores at most \(M_j\) \(a^2\). For \(a>0\), divide by \(a^2\) and take the right derivative at zero. Its actual derivative is the diagonal Hessian entry, so \(\partial_{jj}f(x)\) is at most \(M_j\). Taking the trace proves the pointwise Laplacian bound \(p\) \(M_{\rm av}\). Conversely strong gradient monotonicity along the same coordinate line bounds its difference quotient below by \(m\). Taking the same derivative gives \(m\) at most every diagonal Hessian entry. In the convex case \(m=0\), their sum is nonnegative.

steps.title: Use the genuine Laplacian supremum and complete Lemma 7
steps.body:
Define \(M_{1,\Delta}\) as the supremum of the range of the true Laplacian, divided by \(p\). Its range is nonempty, and the pointwise bound \(p\) \(M_{\rm av}\) makes it bounded above. The defining supremum therefore bounds every Laplacian value and is itself at most \(p\) \(M_{\rm av}\). Dividing by positive \(p\) gives \(M_{1,\Delta}\) at most \(M_{\rm av}\). \(C^{2}\) regularity also makes the Laplacian continuous, as a finite sum of continuous score derivatives. Its nonnegativity and finite pointwise bound prove actual integrability. Under the normalized Gibbs law, the score identity and these pointwise comparisons give exactly

\[\mathbb E_\pi\|\nabla f\|^2=\mathbb E_\pi|\Delta f|\le pM_{1,\Delta}\le pM_{\rm av}.\]

AverageLMC/SGLDEstimator.lean.title: The genuine finite-sum control-variate estimator
AverageLMC/SGLDEstimator.lean.summary: This module constructs the finite-sum potential, the actual uniform component-index probability, and the fixed-point control-variate estimator in the SGLD update. It derives unbiasedness, the exact centered variance identity, the sharp RMS component bound, and all product-space second moments. The anchor is justified by existence and uniqueness of a true minimizer, including its zero gradient.

steps.title: Construct the potential and the uniform index probability
steps.body: The total potential is the finite sum of the component functions. Differentiation commutes with this finite sum, and the gradient identification follows by the inner-product duality map. The uniform index law is counting measure multiplied by 1/\(n\). For \(n\) positive its mass is one. It is a finite measure even at \(n=0\), where the index space is empty. Its Bochner integral is exactly the finite vector sum divided by \(n\); this formula is used for all following index moments.

steps.title: Use the actual fixed-point estimator and prove unbiasedness
steps.body: For an anchor \(x_\star\), define the estimator \(n( abla f_i(x)- abla f_i(x_\star))\). It vanishes at the anchor for every index. Averaging over the uniform index cancels \(n\) and sums the component gradients. If the true total gradient at the anchor is zero, this average is exactly \( abla f(x)\). Thus the paper estimator is unbiased for the gradient of the same potential defining its Gibbs target.

steps.title: Control the full gradient by the total component smoothness
steps.body: Squaring the defining square root gives \(M_{\rm rms}\) squared equal to the average squared exact component-gradient seminorms. The triangle inequality bounds the gradient Lipschitz constant of the sum by the sum of component constants. Finite Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the sum of exact nonnegative seminorms by \(n\) \(M_{\rm rms}\). Replacing each supplied component bound by its proved exact seminorm gives a Lipschitz gradient bound for the full potential with exactly \(n\) \(M_{\rm rms}\). Comparing a strong-convexity lower model with the coordinate upper model then proves \(m\) at most \(n\) \(M_{\rm rms}\). These comparisons justify the dimensionless step-size conditions in the SGLD theorem.

steps.title: Compute and bound the estimator second moment
steps.body:
The uniform average of the squared estimator norm equals \(n\) times the sum of squared component-gradient differences. Each difference is bounded by the component exact seminorm times the distance to the anchor. Square these nonnegative inequalities, sum, and substitute the exact RMS definition. This gives

\[\mathbb E_I\|G_I(x)\|^2\le n^2M_{\rm rms}^2\|x-x_*\|^2.\]

The integral is finite because the index space and measure are finite.

steps.title: Center the error and retain the negative gradient energy
steps.body:
Define the estimator error as \(G_i(x)- abla f(x)\). Unbiasedness proves that its uniform-index expectation is zero. Expanding its squared norm, the cross expectation is the inner product of \( abla f(x)\) with the estimator expectation, hence the squared full-gradient norm. The exact variance identity is therefore

\[\mathbb E_I\|G_I(x)- abla f(x)\|^2=\mathbb E_I\|G_I(x)\|^2-\| abla f(x)\|^2.\]

Dropping the nonnegative final score energy gives the same \(n^2\) RMS distance bound for the centered error. Keeping it is essential for the larger-step one-step SGLD estimates.

steps.title: Supply the measurable product-space error with derived \(L^{2}\) moments
steps.body:
For a random state \(X\) with finite second moment, each component gradient evaluated at \(X\) is \(L^{2}\) by Lipschitz composition. A finite independent index can select these \(L^{2}\) functions: express the selector as the finite sum of component functions times the indicators of the measurable index events. This proves product-space \(L^{2}\) membership of the actual estimator and centered error. Measurability follows by checking each fixed finite-index slice. Fubini then integrates the pointwise variance bound over \(X\), producing

\[\mathbb E\|G_I(X)-\nabla f(X)\|^2\le n^2M_{\rm rms}^2\mathbb E\|X-x_*\|^2.\]

These results supply the genuine random perturbation used by the transport comparison; no error variance is assumed.

steps.title: Construct the unique zero-score minimizer
steps.body: Positive strong convexity gives a quadratic lower bound, so the sublevel set \(f(x)\) at most \(f(0)\) is bounded. Continuity and the extreme-value theorem yield a global minimizer. Fermat theorem makes its actual Frechet derivative and gradient zero. If two points had zero gradients, strong gradient monotonicity would force \(m\) times their squared distance to be at most zero. Since \(m\) is positive, the points coincide. The resulting unique minimizer provides the anchor required by the finite-sum algorithm.

AverageLMC/CompactC2Taylor.lean.title: Weak Gaussian Taylor expansion with exactly two derivatives
AverageLMC/CompactC2Taylor.lean.summary: The potential in the Laplacian theorem (Theorem 2, source th:3) is \(C^{3}\), so its gradient is only \(C^{2}\). These estimates establish the necessary compact-test weak expansion with precisely \(C^{2}\) regularity. A uniformly continuous compact Hessian supplies a freely small quadratic remainder plus a cubic bound; a third derivative of the test is never assumed. The Gaussian averaging requires only a second moment of the random drift.

steps.title: Express the remainder using a genuine Hessian difference
steps.body: Restrict the test to the line \(x+t\) \(v\). The ordinary Taylor theorem with first-order polynomial and second derivative remainder gives a point \(u\) strictly between zero and one. The first derivative on this line is the Frechet derivative applied to \(v\); the second derivative is the actual second Frechet derivative applied twice to \(v\). Subtract the quadratic Taylor term at \(x\). The remaining error is exactly one half of the difference between the Hessians at \(x+u\) \(v\) and \(x\), evaluated twice on \(v\).

steps.title: Use uniform Hessian continuity without a third derivative
steps.body:
A compactly supported \(C^{2}\) test has a continuous compactly supported Hessian, hence a uniformly continuous and bounded Hessian. Given \(\eta\) positive, choose \(\delta\) so that Hessian differences at distance less than \(\delta\) are below \(2\eta\). If the displacement norm is below \(\delta\), the segment remainder is at most \(\eta\) times its squared norm. For larger displacements, the uniform Hessian bound gives a quadratic error, which is bounded by a fixed cubic multiple because the displacement norm is at least \(\delta\). Combining the cases proves

\[|R_2(x,v)|\le\eta\|v\|^2+C_\eta\|v\|^3.\]

The same bounded Hessian proves that the actual gradient of the compact \(C^{2}\) test is Lipschitz.

steps.title: Separate the deterministic drift from Gaussian noise
steps.body:
Expand the test first at the Gaussian perturbation alone. Its linear term averages to zero and its quadratic term averages to \(h\) times the true Laplacian. Integrating the \(C^{2}\) remainder uses the exact Gaussian second moment and finite Gaussian third moment. Choose \(\eta\) small enough that the quadratic Gaussian contribution is at most \(\varepsilon\) \(h\). Insert the deterministic \(hv\) shift afterward using the first-order Lipschitz-gradient remainder. This contributes only \(h^2\) times the squared drift norm and a mixed \(h^{3/2}\) term. For \(h\) at most one, their sum is bounded by

\[h(\varepsilon+K_\varepsilon\sqrt h)(1+\|v\|^2).\]

The bound is uniform in the center, drift and admissible step size. No third moment of the drift is required.

steps.title: Lift the uniform bound through bounded past weights
steps.body: The \(C^{2}\) Laplacian is continuous as a finite sum of continuous second derivatives. This makes the entire weak residual measurable for measurable random centers and drifts. If the past weight has absolute value at most \(A\) almost everywhere, multiply the pointwise residual bound by \(A\) and integrate. Square integrability of the random drift makes the majorant integrable. The resulting bound is \(Ah(\varepsilon+K\sqrt h)\) times one plus the drift second moment. The fixed-\(K\) version retains a supplied uniform pointwise constant unchanged, so the same constant can be used across every Euler mesh and mesh state.

AverageLMC/GibbsScoreCutoff.lean.title: Compact \(C^{2}\) approximation of the actual Gibbs score and generator
AverageLMC/GibbsScoreCutoff.lean.summary:
Smooth radial cutoffs turn an unbounded coordinate of the potential gradient into compact \(C^{2}\) tests. Both the cut-off scores and their true Langevin generators converge in Gibbs \(L^{2}\). The proof derives all score moments from their sub-Gaussian MGFs, controls the product-generator cross terms using exactly the Laplacian-gradient assumption, and applies dominated convergence. This justifies extending compact-test Dynkin identities to the actual score under the paper \(C^{3}\) potential assumption.

Write the genuine scalar generator and vector score generator as

\[g= abla f,\qquad \mathcal L\phi=\Delta\phi-\langle g, abla\phi angle,\qquad G= abla\Delta f-Dg\,g.\]

There are compact \(C^{2}\) coordinate tests, with \(\Phi_n=(\phi_{n,j})_{j=1}^p\) and \(\mathcal L\Phi_n=(\mathcal L\phi_{n,j})_{j=1}^p\), for which every displayed vector belongs to Gibbs \(L^{2}\) and

\[\phi_{n,j}\in C_c^2(\mathbb R^p),\qquad \int\!\|\Phi_n-g\|^2\,d\pi\longrightarrow0,\qquad \int\!\|\mathcal L\Phi_n-G\|^2\,d\pi\longrightarrow0.\]

steps.title: Build an expanding smooth radial cutoff family
steps.body: The \(n\)th bump equals one on the ball of radius \(n+1\) and has support inside radius \(2(n+1)\). It is smooth, compactly supported, and takes values in the interval from zero to one. It is exactly one fixed unit-scale bump composed with multiplication by \(1/(n+1)\). At every fixed spatial point, all sufficiently large cutoffs are identically one in a neighborhood of that point.

steps.title: Bound the first and second cutoff derivatives uniformly
steps.body: The fixed compact smooth bump has bounded derivatives through order two. Rescaling by \(1/(n+1)\) multiplies its \(k\)th derivative by that scalar to the \(k\)th power, which is at most one. Hence a common constant bounds the first two derivative norms for every cutoff. Gradient duality converts the first derivative bound into a gradient bound. Expanding the Laplacian in the canonical orthonormal basis bounds its absolute value by \(p\) times the same constant.

steps.title: Derive every finite Gibbs score moment
steps.body: Each true coordinate of the Gibbs score has the existing Gaussian MGF bound obtained by translation of the density. Sub-Gaussianity supplies all finite scalar moments. Finite-dimensional coordinate membership then proves \(L^{q}\) membership of the entire actual gradient for every finite exponent \(q\). In particular its fourth moment is finite, so one plus its squared norm belongs to Gibbs \(L^{2}\).

steps.title: Preserve compact \(C^{2}\) regularity and local generator equality
steps.body: Multiply a \(C^{2}\) test by the smooth radial cutoff. The product is \(C^{2}\) and has compact support. Because the cutoff is eventually locally one at a fixed point, the products eventually agree with the original test on a neighborhood. Their Frechet derivatives and Laplacians therefore agree there as well. The genuine Langevin generators consequently become pointwise equal. This uses locality of the actual derivatives rather than an assumed approximation identity.

steps.title: Prove dominated \(L^{2}\) convergence for the eventual equalities
steps.body: If every approximation and its limit are bounded in absolute value by a common \(L^{2}\) function \(B\), their squared differences are bounded by 4 \(B^2\). Eventual pointwise equality makes those differences tend to zero. The ordinary dominated convergence theorem then proves convergence of their actual squared integrals to zero. The module also proves continuity of the actual scalar Langevin generator for \(C^{2}\) tests and the bound \(M\) on the gradient norm of every score coordinate.

steps.title: Control the cutoff generator without a bounded third derivative
steps.body: The generator product rule gives the cutoff times the original score generator, the score coordinate times the cutoff generator, and twice the inner product of their gradients. The true score-coordinate generator is the corresponding coordinate of \( abla\Delta f-D( abla f) abla f\). The first term is bounded by the printed Laplacian-gradient condition and the second by \(M\) times the score norm. Uniform cutoff gradient and Laplacian bounds control the remaining terms by a common constant times one plus the squared score norm. This is a genuine Gibbs \(L^{2}\) majorant by the already derived fourth score moment.

steps.title: Produce compact approximations for the real score Dynkin formula
steps.body: For each coordinate \(j\), choose the compact \(C^{2}\) tests equal to the cutoff times the \(j\)th actual gradient coordinate. The score cutoffs are dominated by the score norm. Their true generators are dominated by the common \(L^{2}\) majorant just constructed. Both sequences eventually agree pointwise with their targets. Applying the squared-integral dominated convergence principle twice yields convergence in Gibbs \(L^{2}\) of the tests to the coordinate score and of their generators to the corresponding coordinate of the actual gradient generator. Every normalization and moment assumption needed here follows from finite Gibbs partition, Lipschitz gradient, and the source \(C^{3}\) Laplacian-gradient condition.

steps.title: Assemble one vector approximation with explicit \(L^{2}\) membership
steps.body: Choose the proved scalar approximation for each of the finitely many coordinates and place them in the Euclidean coordinate vector. Each compact test and its compact continuous generator is bounded, hence belongs to Gibbs \(L^{2}\). The target generator belongs to Gibbs \(L^{2}\) because its norm is at most \(M\) times the true score norm plus the fixed Laplacian-gradient bound. Expanding the squared Euclidean error as a finite sum of squared coordinate errors identifies its integral with the sum of the scalar squared integrals. Finite-sum limit continuity proves convergence of both vector errors to zero. The packaged result includes \(L^{2}\) membership of every vector approximant and both actual targets, so later Cauchy-Schwarz arguments do not assume an unproved moment.

AverageLMC/PathwiseEnergy.lean.title: Quadratic integrability and exact energy of the synchronous process
AverageLMC/PathwiseEnergy.lean.summary:
All expectations and derivatives in the stochastic proof are justified on the actual space of square-integrable random variables. A smooth potential need not be globally Lipschitz: its quadratic growth is the correct condition here. The common additive noise cancels before the squared error is differentiated.

Writing \(\langle U,V\rangle_{L^2}=\mathbb E\langle U,V\rangle\), strong convexity and the common-noise integral equation give

\[2\langle X-Y,\nabla f(Y)\rangle_{L^2}\le 2\bigl(\mathbb Ef(X)-\mathbb Ef(Y)\bigr)-m\|X-Y\|_{L^2}^{2}.\] \[\|X+B_h-Y_h\|_{L^2}^{2}=\|X-Y_0\|_{L^2}^{2}+2\int_0^h\langle X+B_t-Y_t,\nabla f(Y_t)\rangle_{L^2}\,dt.\]

steps.title: Smooth potentials are integrable on \(L^{2}\)
steps.body: Apply the quadratic upper model both to \(f\) and to \(-f\) at zero. These two bounds control the absolute value of \(f(x)\) by the sum of \(|f(0)|\), the product of the initial gradient norm and \(\|x\|\), and \(L\|x\|^{2}/2\). A square-integrable random vector has integrable norm and squared norm, so comparison proves integrability of \(f\) evaluated at its \(L^{2}\) representative. The second theorem transfers the result from the quotient-space representative to any supplied random vector with finite second moment by its almost-everywhere equality with the canonical square-integrable representative.

steps.title: Integrate the strong supporting plane
steps.body: At each outcome, strong convexity gives \(f(X)-f(Y)\) at least the inner product of \(\nabla f(Y)\) with \(X-Y\) plus \(m\|X-Y\|^{2}/2\). Every scalar term is integrable by quadratic growth, and the inner product of two \(L^{2}\) vectors is integrable by the \(L^{2}\) Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Integration, the definition of the \(L^{2}\) inner product, and the exact squared-norm integral identity give the supporting-plane inequality on \(L^{2}\) itself. The lifted vector field is the actual gradient applied pointwise, rather than a supplied random drift.

steps.title: Differentiate after the common noise cancels
steps.body: For a continuous vector field \(g\), the primitive \(A+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds\) has derivative \(g(t)\). The derivative of its squared Hilbert norm is twice its inner product with \(g(t)\); the fundamental theorem of calculus proves the displayed exact energy identity. In the Langevin integral equation, \(X+B(t)-Y(t)\) equals \(X-Y(0)+\int_0^t\nabla f(Y(s))\,ds\) because the same \(B\) drives both processes. Substitute this expression into the Hilbert identity. No derivative of a Brownian path and no stochastic isometry is assumed.

AverageLMC/GaussianPerturbation.lean.title: Random-center smoothing and the integrated Gaussian energy bound
AverageLMC/GaussianPerturbation.lean.summary:
This module carries out the expectation and time-integration steps used in the improved one-step estimate. Independence promotes a deterministic smoothing estimate to a random center; strong convexity and orthogonality then give the exact Gaussian energy constant.

The energy theorem uses an affine upper bound for the expected potential difference, the exact Brownian increment moment, orthogonality, and a common lower bound \(w\) for \(\|X+B_h-Y_t\|_{L^2}^2\). Its key input and conclusion are

\[\mathbb Ef(X+B_t)-\mathbb Ef(Y_t)\le a+bt\qquad(0\le t\le h).\] \[(1+mh)w\le\|X-Y_0\|_{L^2}^{2}+2ha+h^2b+mh^2d.\]

steps.title: Promote smoothing to an independent random center
steps.body: For independent \(L^{2}\) vectors \(X\) and \(Z\), their joint pushforward measure is the product of their marginal laws. The function \(F(x,z)=f(x+cz)-f(x)\) is continuous and integrable under this joint law because both arguments have finite second moment and \(f\) has quadratic growth. The pushforward identity and Fubini turn its expectation into the iterated integral. Integrate the pointwise smoothing bound over the law of \(X\), which is a probability measure, to retain the same constant. Finally use almost-everywhere representatives to identify the pointwise sum with the sum in \(L^{2}\).

steps.title: Integrate strong convexity with the future-noise correction
steps.body: Let \(w\) be a common lower bound for the squared coupling costs between \(X+B(h)\) and the stationary comparison \(Y(t)\). Orthogonality expands the latter cost exactly as \(\|X+B(t)-Y(t)\|^{2}+2(h-t)d\). Integrate the strong supporting-plane bound, using an affine upper bound \(a+b\) \(t\) for the potential expectation difference. The integrand is bounded by \(2a+2mhd-mw+(2b-2md)t\). Its explicit integral is \(2ha+mh^{2}d-mhw+h^{2}b\). Combine this with the exact synchronous energy identity and the endpoint coupling bound to obtain \((1+mh)w\le \|X-Y(0)\|^{2}+2ha+h^{2}b+mh^{2}d\). Every input involving noise or stationarity is discharged for the actual Gaussian step by the canonical construction in the following modules.

AverageLMC/GaussianBrownian.lean.title: Exact future Brownian moments and derived orthogonality
AverageLMC/GaussianBrownian.lean.summary:
The improved energy estimate uses the actual Brownian process underlying the stationary Langevin solution. Its future increments have exact moments, and their orthogonality to the coupled past is derived from independence and adaptedness.

For the scaled noise \(B_t=\sqrt2W_t\), genuine independence and the constructed adapted integral solution imply, for \(0\le t\le h\),

\[\mathbb E(B_h-B_t)=0,\qquad\|B_h-B_t\|_{L^2}^{2}=2(h-t)p.\] \[\langle X+B_t-Y_t,\,B_h-B_t\rangle_{L^2}=0.\]

steps.title: Center and measure future Brownian noise
steps.body: The Langevin additive noise is \(\sqrt 2\) times a Brownian increment. Its expectation vanishes at every time, so the expectation of a future difference also vanishes. Algebraically, the difference between the noises at \(h\) and \(t\) is the additive noise over the segment starting at \(t\) with length \(h-t\). The existing exact Brownian \(L^{2}\) norm formula therefore gives its squared norm as \(2(h-t)d\). This uses the true elapsed-time Gaussian variance and covers the endpoint \(t=h\).

steps.title: Derive the orthogonality of the actual error
steps.body: The complete initial state and stopped Brownian past are independent of the future Brownian increment. Projection onto the initial-state and current-noise coordinates gives zero \(L^{2}\) inner product with each of them because the future increment is centered. For \(Y(t)\), the natural-past measurability of the actual integral solution has already been proved by the invariant-subspace construction; applying it to the identity vector field gives the same zero inner product. Subtract and add the three identities to prove that \(X+B(t)-Y(t)\) is orthogonal to \(B(h)-B(t)\). No stochastic-error orthogonality condition is assumed in the final LMC theorem.

AverageLMC/GaussianCanonical.lean.title: Construct the stationary coupling of one actual Gaussian LMC step
AverageLMC/GaussianCanonical.lean.summary:
The theorem starts from an arbitrary finite-cost initial coupling and the original smooth strongly convex potential. It constructs the independent Brownian extension, the actual integral solution, its stationary Gibbs law, and the exact Gaussian output law. The only local auxiliary input is the coordinate smoothing theorem proved separately.

Let \(\gamma\) be any finite-cost coupling of \( u\) and \(\pi\), with \(C_\gamma^2=\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\gamma\). The canonical independent Brownian extension realizes the actual update

\[\vartheta^+=\vartheta-h abla f(\vartheta)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi,\qquad\xi\sim N(0,I_p),\quad\xi\perp\!\!\!\perp\vartheta.\] \[(1+mh)W_2^2( u^+,\pi)\le(1-mh)C_\gamma^2+(M_{ m av}+m)h^2p+h^2(hL-1)\int\| abla f(x)\|^2\,d u(x).\]

steps.title: Construct, identify and estimate the actual transition
steps.body: Extend the initial coupling by the explicit canonical product Brownian probability space. Its initial algorithm state \(X\) has law \(\mu\) and its reference state \(Z\) has the true Gibbs law. The Lipschitz drift constructs a continuous \(L^{2}\) Langevin integral solution; stationarity follows from the already proved Gibbs-stationarity theorem. Independent scalar Brownian paths provide independent standard Gaussian innovations at every positive time. The algorithm center \(A=X-h\nabla f(X)\) is a measurable function of the initial state, so it remains independent of those innovations. The endpoint \(A+B(h)\) has exactly the ordinary Gaussian LMC transition law. Local coordinate smoothing at \(A\) gives the affine potential bound needed by the Gaussian energy theorem. Integrated strong convexity controls \(\|A-Z\|^{2}\), and integrated deterministic descent controls \(\mathbb E f(A)-\mathbb E f(X)\). These potential terms cancel. Identifying the lifted gradient norm with the score moment under \(\mu\) leaves precisely \((1-mh)\) times the initial coupling cost squared, \((M_{\mathrm{av}}+m)h^{2}d\), and \(h^2(hL-1)\) times the score second moment. Output transport finiteness follows from the constructed \(L^{2}\) coupling before any real-valued distance is used.

AverageLMC/GaussianLMC.lean.title: The exact averaged-smoothness one-step LMC theorem
AverageLMC/GaussianLMC.lean.summary:
This is Theorem 1, claim 1, for the actual Gaussian Markov transition and the literal average coordinate Taylor supremum. It assumes no coupling recurrence, stationary-reference bundle, or desired convergence estimate.

For the actual independent Gaussian step, \(M_{ m av}\) is the paper's average of the exact coordinate constants, and \(L\) is the global gradient Lipschitz constant. Theorem 1's local inequality is

A continuously differentiable derivative map loses one order of regularity, and evaluation at a fixed vector preserves the remaining regularity. Differentiating that evaluation identifies a second directional derivative with the actual second Fréchet derivative applied to the two directions. Schwarz symmetry for \(C^{2}\) functions then commutes the two directional derivatives as functions of the base point. These statements are proved for arbitrary real normed spaces, before choosing Euclidean coordinates.

steps.title: Commute the needed three derivatives without analyticity
steps.body: For a \(C^{3}\) potential, first commute the two inner directional derivatives using \(C^{2}\) symmetry of \(f\). Then commute the outer pair using \(C^{2}\) symmetry of one first directional derivative. This gives \(D_{u}D_{u}D_{v}f=D_{v}D_{u}D_{u}f\). The argument establishes exactly the third-order permutation needed for the Laplacian and avoids any appeal to an analytic-only iterated-derivative permutation theorem.

The \(j\)th coordinate of the actual gradient equals the directional derivative along \(e_j\) by the gradient–Fréchet-derivative identity. A finite sum of differentiable scalar functions can be differentiated term by term. The \(j\)th coordinate of \(\nabla \Delta f\) is \(D_j\) of the finite Laplacian sum, namely the sum of \(D_jD_iD_i f\). Apply the proved third-derivative commutation term by term, then use equality of all Euclidean coordinates to obtain the full vector identity.

The Riesz representation of its derivative gives continuity of \( abla \Delta f\); evaluation of the continuous Hessian on the continuous gradient gives continuity of the second term. The proved vector commutation identity identifies this field exactly with \(\Delta ( abla f)-D( abla f) abla f\), the Langevin generator applied to \( abla f\).

The first representative has norm at most \(M_\Delta \sqrt p\); the second has norm at most \(L\) times the lifted score norm. AverageLMC/SmoothnessScaling.lean.title: Exact scaling of coordinate smoothness constants
